name: Ananias
title: Member of the early church in Jerusalem
summary:
Ananias belonged to the first Christian congregation in Jerusalem and is known from a dramatic event recorded in Acts.  
Together with his wife Sapphira, he sold a property, but the couple deliberately withheld part of the sale proceeds yet still presented their gift as if it represented the full amount.  
When the apostle Peter, through the insight of the Holy Spirit, exposed this deception, he emphasized that Ananias had not only lied to people but to God himself.  
Immediately after Peter’s confrontation, Ananias fell down dead.  
This event, in which Sapphira suffered the same fate shortly afterward, marks a decisive moment in the history of the young church.  
It clearly shows that God’s holiness demands sincerity and truthfulness within the community of believers, and it inspired deep reverence both among Christians and in their surroundings.

keyEvents.title: Sale of property and withholding of funds
keyEvents.description: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of property, but agreed between themselves to keep back part of the proceeds for themselves while pretending to give the entire amount to the apostles.

keyEvents.title: Peter's confrontation
keyEvents.description: The apostle Peter, led by the Holy Spirit, saw through the deception and confronted Ananias. Peter pointed out that Ananias had not lied to men but to God himself.

keyEvents.title: Ananias' sudden death
keyEvents.description: As soon as Ananias heard Peter's words, he fell down and died. Great fear seized all who heard about it, and young men came, wrapped him up, carried him out, and buried him.

keyEvents.title: Sapphira's death
keyEvents.description: About three hours later Sapphira came in, not knowing what had happened to her husband. She repeated the same lie to Peter and also fell down dead.

keyEvents.title: Reverence in the Church
keyEvents.description: After the death of Ananias and Sapphira, great fear came over the whole church and all who heard about it, underscoring the seriousness of living truthfully before God.

versions.summary: Ananias was a member of the early Christian church in Jerusalem who, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a property but withheld part of the proceeds while claiming to give everything to the apostles. When Peter confronted him about the lie, Ananias fell down dead, causing great fear throughout the church.
versions.title: Deceitful Believers in the Early Church
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Deceitful Believer in the Early Church' is negatively charged and somewhat one-sided. A more neutral and descriptive title would have been better, e.g., 'Member of the Early Church in Jerusalem'.; [major] The role 'disciple' is imprecise. Ananias was not a disciple in the technical sense (one of the twelve), but a member/believer in the early church. A more appropriate role would be 'believer' or 'member of the early church'.; [minor] The summary is good, but could advantageously mention the theological significance of the event – that it illustrates God's holiness and the seriousness of lying to the Holy Spirit.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are several interesting linguistic, theological, and historical aspects of this account that should be illuminated, such as the meaning of the name, the theological parallel to Achan in the OT, and the practice of communal ownership in the early church.

versions.summary: Ananias was a member of the early Christian church in Jerusalem who, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a property but withheld part of the proceeds while claiming to give the full amount to the apostles. When the apostle Peter, led by the Holy Spirit, confronted him about the lie, Ananias fell down dead. This event illustrates the seriousness of lying to the Holy Spirit and God's holiness in the newborn church, creating great reverence among believers.

versions.reason: [minor] The summary is well-written and theologically correct, but it closely resembles the previous version (version 1). It should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish itself from the earlier iteration. A slightly different angle and structure would strengthen its profile.; [minor] The role 'believer in the early church' is accurate, but one could also add 'property owner' as a supplementary role, since this is relevant to the event that characterizes him.; [minor] The fourth footnote regarding the term 'the vessel' is somewhat speculative. In Jewish tradition, the term 'the vessel' is primarily linked to specific transgressions in the Torah and is not necessarily used directly concerning events in the New Testament. The wording should be nuanced to avoid presenting this as an established connection.

footnotes.text: The name Ananias (Greek: Ananias, Hebrew: Chananja) means 'the Lord is gracious' or 'Yahweh has shown grace.' There is a striking contrast between the meaning of the name and the action for which this person is best known in Acts.

The account of Ananias and Sapphira has clear theological parallels to the story of Achan in Joshua 7, where Achan withheld some of the devoted things after the conquest of Jericho and was punished with death. Both events mark the beginning of a new phase in God's redemptive history and emphasize God's holiness within the covenant community.

The early church in Jerusalem practiced a form of voluntary sharing, where believers sold property and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet for distribution (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–37). Peter's words in Acts 5:4 emphasize that this was entirely voluntary—the sin lay not in keeping money, but in deceiving God and the church.

Barnabas's generous act of selling a field and giving the full amount to the apostles (Acts 4:36–37) serves as a deliberate literary contrast to the deceit of Ananias and Sapphira. Luke places these two accounts one after the other to highlight the difference between genuine and false devotion in the early church.

In rabbinic and Jewish thought, deliberate lying against God was seen as a particularly serious offense. The sudden death of Ananias and Sapphira has been understood as an expression of divine judgment, and in early church teaching, this event was frequently used as a warning against hypocrisy and as an example of the Holy Spirit's authority in the church.

Archaeological findings from first-century Jerusalem show that property transactions were common, with many houses and plots being bought and sold. The social pressure within the early church to demonstrate generosity may have contributed to Ananias and Sapphira's temptation to appear more generous than they actually were.
